Content:
A basis of a subspace [MATH: U] (in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n]) is a set of vectors in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] that is linearly independent and spans [MATH: U.]

Content:
For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
To find a basis of [MATH: U,] we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans [MATH: U.]

Content:
Watch out! The set
[MATH: [1; 0]]
is not a basis of [MATH: U.] It's true that this set spans [MATH: U,] but the vectors in this set are not linearly independent. In particular, the vector [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}_3] can be written as a linear combination of [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [− 1; 3]]

Content:
To find a basis of [MATH: U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},] we can start with [MATH: \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},] but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}] because it can be written as a linear combination of [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.]

Content:
We are left with the set

[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span [MATH: U.] That is to say,

Content:
[MATH: U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.]

Content:
Therefore, the set [MATH: \mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}] is a basis of [MATH: U.]

Content:
Note: To see that the vectors [MATH: \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}] still span [MATH: U,] first note that any vector [MATH: \mathbf{b} \in U] can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}]

Content:
Since [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},] then we must have
[MATH: b|= x_{1}a_{1} + x_{2}a_{2} + x_{3}(− a_{1} + 3a_{2}); = (x_{1} − x_{3})a_{1} + (x_{2} + 3x_{3})a_{2},]
which shows that [MATH: \mathbf{b}] can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.]

Content:
Therefore, we can conclude that the set [MATH: \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}] spans the subspace [MATH: U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A basis of a subspace [MATH: U] (in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n]) is a set of vectors in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] that is linearly independent and spans [MATH: U.]

Content:
For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
To find a basis of [MATH: U,] we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans [MATH: U.]

Content:
Watch out! The set
[MATH: [1; 0]]
is not a basis of [MATH: U.] It's true that this set spans [MATH: U,] but the vectors in this set are not linearly independent. In particular, the vector [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}_3] can be written as a linear combination of [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [− 1; 3]]

Content:
To find a basis of [MATH: U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},] we can start with [MATH: \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},] but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}] because it can be written as a linear combination of [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.]

Content:
We are left with the set

Content:
[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span [MATH: U.] That is to say,

Content:
[MATH: U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.]

Content:
Therefore, the set [MATH: \mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}] is a basis of [MATH: U.]

Content:
Note: To see that the vectors [MATH: \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}] still span [MATH: U,] first note that any vector [MATH: \mathbf{b} \in U] can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}]

Content:
Since [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},] then we must have
[MATH: b|= x_{1}a_{1} + x_{2}a_{2} + x_{3}(− a_{1} + 3a_{2}); = (x_{1} − x_{3})a_{1} + (x_{2} + 3x_{3})a_{2},]
which shows that [MATH: \mathbf{b}] can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.]

Content:
Therefore, we can conclude that the set [MATH: \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}] spans the subspace [MATH: U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection

Example Prompt:
Consider the vectors [MATH: [2; 3]] and [MATH: [1; 1]] Find a basis of [MATH: S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}] by inspection.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that a basis of [MATH: S] is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans [MATH: S.]

From the given vectors, we can see that [MATH: \mathbf{a}_2] is a linear combination of vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{a}_3\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \mathbf{a}_2=1\cdot \mathbf{a}_1+1\cdot \mathbf{a}_3]

Consequently, the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}_2] can be removed from [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}] without changing the span. So [MATH: S = \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}] is spanned by just [MATH: \{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\}.]

Lastly, note that [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{a}_3] are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set [MATH: \{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\}] is a linearly independent set that spans [MATH: S.]

Therefore, a basis of [MATH: S] is [MATH: \{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\},] that is to say,

[MATH: [2; 3]]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Finding a Basis by Identifying Pivot Columns

Content:
In the previous example, it was easy to see that one vector was a linear combination of the others. But what can we do when it's not so easy to tell? For example, consider the subspace

Content:
[MATH: [1; − 2]]

Content:
To find a subset of linearly independent vectors, we can put the vectors in a matrix and compute the reduced row echelon form:

Content:
[MATH: =[1|− 1|− 1; − 2|3|7]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + 2R_{1}; ∼[1|− 1|− 1; 0|1|5]|R_{1}|:=R_{1} + R_{2}; ∼[1|0|4; 0|1|5]]

Content:
The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent (or redundant) vectors that can be removed. Here, the [MATH: 1]st and [MATH: 2]nd columns are pivot columns, while the [MATH: 3]rd column is a non-pivot column.

Content:
But watch out! We need to pick the pivot columns from the original matrix, not from the reduced one.

Content:
The [MATH: 1]st and [MATH: 2]nd columns from the original matrix are [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{a}_2.] So, a basis of [MATH: U] is [MATH: \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},] that is to say,

Content:
[MATH: [1; − 2]]

Item 6 — Example: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns

Example Prompt:
Consider the vectors [MATH: [5; 2]] [MATH: [10; 4]] and [MATH: [15; 5]] Find a basis of [MATH: S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
